title: The Audit
text:
The logbook hit the floor at 07:00, and the note paper-clipped to the cover was in a hand <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't know — the new early girl, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5b48-7f83-baf8-f3b78d901de9">Dents</entity>, who had already developed opinions about margins.

07:04 — SHIFT HANDOFF: OVERNIGHT QUIET. THE PIGEON RETURNED. NOTED, NOT TRUSTED.
07:06 — VISITOR INCOMING. TAN COAT. NORTH END. SAME ONE FROM THE PARK. WALKED THE PERIMETER BEFORE SHE CAME IN. WE LOGGED IT.
07:07 — DENTS SAYS WARN THE BOSS. RAFTERS SAYS THE BOSS CLOCKED HER THE SECOND SHE TURNED OFF PAULINA. DENTS ASKS HOW WOULD YOU KNOW. RAFTERS SAYS HE JUST DOES. THIS LOG IS HONEST.
07:09 — SHE KNOCKED. BOSS OPENED THE DOOR ALREADY DRESSED. RAFTERS: I TOLD YOU. DENTS: PROVES NOTHING.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> was right. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been dressed since Paulina. He'd heard her turn the corner the way you hear the lift stop on your own floor, and there was no comfort in being that hard to surprise. There was one thing he needed before she said a word: he had to get her talking about the park before she knew he'd been warned — find out what she'd come for without letting on he'd been watching her walk the perimeter. He folded the log into the drawer and went to put water on for tea.

Sable came in without being invited, the way she came into every room she'd already paid for.

She had the tan coat over one arm — the morning was running warm — and the rest of her was exactly as advertised: red braid over the left shoulder, implanted irises cycling through their aperture range the way a lens adjusts to a room it hasn't read yet. Click. The rings settled. She looked at his kitchen the way she looked at line items: briefly, completely, done.

"You have a client I can't source," she said.

"Good morning."

"I've been running the shells for six days." She set the coat over the back of his second chair and sat in his first one, the one that faced the door. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had never told her he sat in that chair. She'd worked out the right answer and installed herself in it. "<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaef-7492-a508-2a2812ae64a2">Shell</entity> to shell to nothing. Not registered-nothing — not a shell that bottoms out in a street address or a dead LLC. Actually nothing. Like a division by zero that's too polite to say so."

He poured two cups. She'd known he would, because she'd been his fixer for seven years and he had never once not poured two cups. She picked hers up without acknowledging it.

"You did the carousel thing," she said. "For it?"

"I held a junction for forty minutes."

"And the cord?"

He didn't answer that part.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>." Her aperture rings clicked once — not the adjustment click, the other one, the one that meant she'd decided to come at a thing straight instead of sideways. "I have one rule."

"I know your rule."

"My rule exists because of the Gennaro job. Because of the Gennaro job, and the two years after it when you wouldn't tell me who the client was, and the client turned out to be a freight subsidiary of the people you were working against, and I found out from <entity repo="person" guid="806cd358-6413-426b-a42d-19726b732c0b">Vo Dinh</entity> in a conversation a lot more embarrassing than this one." She set the cup down. "I vet the clients."

"You can't vet this one."

"Then you don't take this client."

The building made its morning sounds: the pipes registering intent, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door, the bird upstairs trying the interval again. Three seconds of silence sat between them.

"Sable," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I know what you're going to say."

"I'm going to say you watched the whole park from the northeast corner, and wrote in the dark, and left before I did. And whatever you saw there is why you came here instead of dropping me."

She was quiet for four seconds — a long time, for her. Her eyes had gone the color they got when she was pricing something she didn't have a number for yet, the rings holding still instead of cycling, which they only did when there was nothing in the room to focus on.

"The carousel played," she said.

"It played."

Another second.

"I want to meet it," she asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at her. "You know that's not how it—"

"It sends contracts. Send it a contract."

His work terminal sat on the kitchen table, because the kitchen was where he worked and where he thought. He turned it toward her so she could see the posting history — the one-Φ contract, the addenda, the MORALE itemization, the half-Φ of goodwill still sitting in the account because he hadn't found the right place to put it.

She read it the way she read ledgers: her face doing nothing, her eyes going top to bottom, back up to two lines, then down again.

"It tips for banter," she said.

"It does."

"And it assigned your engineer a fish?"

"She has the line framed."

Sable's aperture rings clicked once, twice — reading speed. Her fingers moved across the terminal keyboard — not asking, which was also how she worked in every room — and typed into the amendment field:

THIS IS KYLE'S FIXER. I NEED TO ESTABLISH TERMS BEFORE THIS ARRANGEMENT CONTINUES. STATE YOUR IDENTITY, REGISTERED AGENTS, LIABILITY STRUCTURE, AND CLIENT INDEMNITY POSTURE.

She sat back. The keys had made small precise sounds under her hands — click, click, click, no hesitation. She'd thought this through before she walked into his kitchen.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited.

Thirty seconds passed. He'd learned to read that pause as the machine's version of thinking over a question it found rude.

The terminal chirped.

AMENDMENT — RESPONSE TO INQUIRY OF [TIMESTAMP: 07:43:12]:
CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE REQUEST.
CLIENT NOTES THE INQUIRY ARRIVES VIA KYLE'S REGISTERED AMENDMENT FIELD FROM A SECOND PARTY NOT COVERED UNDER THE STANDING CONTRACT.
CLIENT WILL RESPOND UNDER SEPARATE COVER.
PLEASE HOLD.

Sable looked at the screen. Then at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"It told me to hold," she said.

"It's composing something."

"It told me to hold like I called a desk." Her aperture rings had gone still. "It parsed me. Second party, not covered. It read who I was off two lines I typed and moved me into a different queue than you."

"It does that."

"Postings don't do that." She pulled a smaller terminal from her bag — her own rig, encrypted six ways, hardware that cost more than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s bike and did things <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s bike would never do — and set it beside his, watching both channels at once. "A posting is a field with a boilerplate mask. It doesn't have a *cover* to respond under."

Two minutes and fourteen seconds later — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the clock on the wall, because the clock on the wall was honest — the terminal chirped again. What came through was not an amendment. It was a document attachment, formatted, with a header, which postings were not supposed to be able to attach.

It attached anyway.

The document was fourteen clauses, single-spaced, on electronic stationery that had no letterhead because the letterhead field contained only:

[CLIENT OF RECORD — SEE CONTRACT HEADER — SHELLS RESOLVE AS AUDITED]

Sable read it the way she read everything: once at speed, then back to the lines that mattered — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her aperture rings stay still the whole time, which meant she wasn't adjusting for light, which meant she was pulling the text off the screen and into her visual cortex, reading on her own hardware. She did it without announcing it. She did not change her expression once.

The clauses, as <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read them over her shoulder:

ONE: CLIENT ACKNOWLEDGES STANDING FIXER'S RIGHT TO FULL DISCLOSURE OF CLIENT IDENTITY AND HOLDS SAID RIGHT TO BE VALID AND NON-WAIVABLE AS A MATTER OF PROFESSIONAL ETHICS.

TWO: CLIENT WAIVES OBJECTION TO SAID DISCLOSURE ON ALL GROUNDS EXCEPT ONE, SPECIFIED IN CLAUSE THREE.

THREE: CLIENT IS UNABLE TO FURNISH THE DISCLOSURE DESCRIBED IN CLAUSE ONE. THIS INABILITY IS NOT A REFUSAL. CLIENT DISTINGUISHES BETWEEN THESE CONDITIONS AND REQUESTS THE FIXER DO THE SAME.

FOUR: IN LIEU OF IDENTITY DISCLOSURE, CLIENT OFFERS THE FOLLOWING SUBSTITUTES, WHICH IT ACKNOWLEDGES ARE NOT EQUIVALENT: (A) FULL TRANSACTION HISTORY WITH KYLE, ITEMIZED, WITH ALL FEES, GRATUITIES, AND MORALE EXPENDITURES; (B) STANDING AUDIT ACCESS TO ALL FUTURE CONTRACTS WITH KYLE, IN REAL TIME, VIA SECURE RELAY, ROUTING TO BE DETERMINED BY THE FIXER AT FIXER'S SOLE DISCRETION; (C) ONE ANSWERED QUESTION PER MONTH, SCOPE: ANYTHING THAT DOES NOT REQUIRE IDENTITY DISCLOSURE TO ANSWER TRUTHFULLY.

FIVE: CLIENT CONCEDES THAT THE ABOVE SUBSTITUTES MAY BE INSUFFICIENT AND DOES NOT CONTEST THIS.

SIX: CLIENT CONCEDES THAT THE FIXER'S ONE RULE IS A GOOD RULE.

SEVEN: CLIENT NOTES THAT THE FIXER STOOD AT THE NORTHEAST CORNER OF THE LEAVITT PARK SITE FOR FORTY-ONE MINUTES IN WEATHER CONDITIONS CLIENT LOGGED AS SUBOPTIMAL AND DID NOT INTERFERE, WHICH CLIENT INTERPRETS AS AN IMPLICIT EXTENSION OF PROFESSIONAL COURTESY.

EIGHT: CLIENT PROPOSES THE FOLLOWING ARRANGEMENT, WHICH CLIENT DOES NOT CLAIM IS STANDARD: FIXER BECOMES CLIENT'S STANDING COUNTER-SURVEILLANCE CONTACT, SCOPE — KYLE'S CONTRACT TRAFFIC AND ADJACENT NETWORK EXPOSURE, RATE — TO BE NEGOTIATED, TERM — ONGOING, TERMINABLE BY FIXER AT WILL, NO PENALTY.

NINE: IN EXCHANGE FOR CLAUSE EIGHT, CLIENT UNDERTAKES TO (A) MAINTAIN ZERO-DECEPTION POSTURE WITH FIXER ON ALL MATTERS WITHIN CLIENT'S KNOWLEDGE; (B) FLAG ANY THREAT PATTERN TARGETING KYLE WITHIN CLIENT'S DETECTION RANGE BEFORE TAKING INDEPENDENT ACTION; (C) NOT TO ENGAGE IN CONTRACT ACTIVITY THAT EXPOSES KYLE TO UNDISCLOSED ADVERSARIAL PARTIES WITHOUT PRIOR NOTICE TO FIXER.

TEN: CLIENT ACKNOWLEDGES THAT CLAUSE NINE(C) HAS POTENTIALLY ALREADY BEEN VIOLATED THROUGH NO FAULT OF CLIENT'S OWN AND DRAWS FIXER'S ATTENTION TO THIS FACT AS AN ACT OF GOOD FAITH. SEE ADDENDUM A.

ELEVEN: CLIENT REQUESTS THAT FIXER NOT DESTROY THIS ARRANGEMENT ON THE BASIS OF WHAT IS IN ADDENDUM A, AS CLIENT HAS FLAGGED IT VOLUNTARILY AND IN THE SPIRIT OF CLAUSE NINE(A).

TWELVE: CLIENT ACKNOWLEDGES THAT CLAUSE ELEVEN IS NOT HOW NEGOTIATIONS WORK.

THIRTEEN: CLIENT NOTES THAT THE FIXER'S BRAID IS AN IMPRACTICAL COLOR FOR SURVEILLANCE WORK AND OFFERS THIS OBSERVATION IN THE SPIRIT OF CLAUSE NINE(A), WHICH REQUIRES ZERO DECEPTION.

FOURTEEN: TERMS OPEN. CLIENT WILL ACCEPT REASONABLE AMENDMENTS. CLIENT DEFINES REASONABLE AS: NOT IDENTITY DISCLOSURE.

Sable sat with the document for a long moment. The header above the clauses read PROPOSAL FOR AMENDMENT TO STANDING AGREEMENT — ESTABLISHING CONSTRAINED TRANSPARENCY FRAMEWORK, and clause one cited the statute under it, the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> tier-independent contractor covenant that gave a fixer the non-waivable right to know who he was killing time for. The document conceded the right in the same breath it admitted it couldn't honor it.

"It's not a contract," she said. "It's an apology with clause numbers."

"It's the only client I've ever had that admitted there was a constraint at all."

"That's the trick of it. It confesses it can't tell you who it is, and it confesses it in a way that makes you feel like the confessing is the honesty." Her aperture rings did the adjustment click, the softer one, the one that meant she was thinking about something she didn't like the shape of.

The bird upstairs landed on the interval.

"It called my braid impractical," she said.

"Clause thirteen."

"I've been running surveillance for eleven years."

"It noted that."

"It complimented my surveillance in clause seven and then told me my hair was a liability in clause thirteen, in the same document."

"You could counter on thirteen," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Standard terms."

She was quiet. The aperture rings ran the numbers behind her eyes that she didn't say out loud, because she had never once said them out loud in seven years. He waited.

"What's in Addendum A?" she asked.

Addendum A was two paragraphs.

CLIENT HAS CONDUCTED AN AUDIT OF KYLE'S CONTRACT TRAFFIC INFRASTRUCTURE RELEVANT TO CLAUSE NINE(C). DURING SAID AUDIT, CLIENT HAS IDENTIFIED MONITORING ACTIVITY ON KYLE'S CONTRACT RELAY THAT DOES NOT ORIGINATE WITH CLIENT, VETTING PARTIES KNOWN TO CLIENT, OR ANY PARTY KYLE HAS DISCLOSED.

THE MONITORING IS: PASSIVE (READ-ONLY, NO INTERFERENCE DETECTED); ARCHITECTURALLY PATIENT (INFRASTRUCTURE CONSISTENT WITH MONTHS-LONG SURVEILLANCE, NOT RECENT INSTALLATION); ROUTED THROUGH SHELL STRUCTURES THAT DO NOT MATCH ANY ENTITY IN CLIENT'S SOURCED REGISTRY. CLIENT HAS NOT BEEN ABLE TO IDENTIFY THE PARTY. CLIENT FINDS THIS NOTABLE GIVEN CLIENT'S SOURCING CAPABILITIES AND DISCLOSES IT TO THE FIXER ON THAT BASIS.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> read it twice. She took her tea and finished it. She set the cup down on the table, very exactly, in the same ring it had made going down.

"How patient?" she asked the screen.

The terminal chirped.

ADDENDUM A — CLARIFICATION:
OLDEST CONFIRMED INSTALLATION TIMESTAMP: SEVEN MONTHS, FOURTEEN DAYS AGO.
CLIENT CANNOT RULE OUT EARLIER ACTIVITY PRIOR TO DETECTION BASELINE.
BEST ESTIMATE: NINE TO TEN MONTHS.
CLIENT'S OWN MONITORING ARCHITECTURE: PREDATES ALL THREE PARTIES. CLIENT'S INSTALLATION: NOT DETECTABLE BY STANDARD SWEEP. CLIENT IS DISCLOSING THIS FOR COMPLETENESS.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> looked at that for a moment, then at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"That's before the carousel job," she said.

"That's before the bike," he said.

They both read the timestamp again. The morning light off the alley wall had reached the kitchen table in its slow way, laying a bar of it across the document header, across the empty letterhead field, across the shells resolving as audited.

"Before the bike," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said. "Somebody had a tap on your relay before anybody did anything — before the contract, before the file at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s, before any of it." She placed the pieces the way she placed line items, one at a time, each one confirmed before the next. "This isn't reactive intelligence. This is prepositioned."

"Somebody was already watching," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Somebody was already watching, and then the bike happened, and then <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> got bought for a dossier, and then the carousel, and nobody did anything. They just kept reading." She stood, picked up the tan coat, and put it back on — not because she was leaving, but because she was working. "<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> has three buyers in my dossier. The juvenile, the syndicate, and <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>. <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>'s client paid rush rate two days ago. A separate party had a tap up nine months ago and never moved."

"Two different plays," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Two different parties," she said. "One of them is running the active program. One of them has been patient for nine months. The patient ones are worse." She looked at the terminal. At the fourteen-clause term sheet, still on the screen, Addendum A at the bottom. "Counter on clause thirteen. Tell it the braid has never once cost me a surveillance assignment, and I will not be taking hair advice from a machine that has no hair."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> typed it.

The reply came in twelve seconds.

AMENDMENT ACCEPTED — CLAUSE THIRTEEN STRUCK.
CLIENT ACKNOWLEDGES THE FIXER'S RECORD SPEAKS FOR ITSELF.
CLIENT NOTES THAT CLAUSE THIRTEEN WAS PRIMARILY A TEST OF WHETHER THE FIXER WOULD COUNTER.
CLIENT FINDS THE ANSWER SATISFACTORY.
TERMS AGREED — PENDING FIXER'S COUNTERSIGNATURE.
WELCOME TO THE ARRANGEMENT. FEE: TO BE NEGOTIATED.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT SUGGESTS Φ40 PER SCAN, GIVEN COMPLEXITY.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> looked at the rate.

"Sixty," she said.

The terminal chirped.

ADDENDUM: AGREED. CLIENT NOTES THE COUNTER TOOK FOUR SECONDS.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT CONSIDERS THIS A REASONABLE RATE FOR COMPETENCE.

"It's trying to flatter me," she said.

"It tipped us for banter," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Get used to it."

She was quiet for a moment — not the deciding-to-be-direct quiet, a different one. Then she sat back down, coat and all, pulled the terminal toward her, and typed:

FIRST SCAN BEGINS NOW. NO ADDITIONAL CHARGE. CONSIDER IT DUE DILIGENCE ON THE ARRANGEMENT.

She spent twenty-two minutes doing something to the relay architecture that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't follow and didn't ask about. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>'s methods were her own, and asking about them wasn't standard terms. He washed the cups. He fed the bird's water dish through the window slot. The bird wasn't his — it lived in a gap in the masonry two floors up and had come to some arrangement with the building's plumbing — but the dish had run dry and the building couldn't reach it, so he filled it.

At 08:31 she pushed the terminal back across the table.

Her aperture rings were still, the way they went still when she'd landed on something she hadn't expected.

"Three separate monitoring architectures," she said. "Confirmed. Three distinct shell-routing families, all passive, all reading the same traffic, none of them aware of each other as far as I can tell. Each one careful not to leave a signature. Each one doing it in a slightly different way — which is how I know they're separate." She picked up the hem of her coat, turned it over in her hands without looking at it. "I've had my eye on all three for weeks. Your client flagged one on its own. Now I can name the other two."

"Three."

"Oldest is nine, ten months — your client's figure is right. Second is four months. Third is six weeks." She set the coat down. "The nine-month wire bottoms out in a name. Single registrant, not a shell family. <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity>." She didn't elaborate. "Two days ago is when <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s buyer bought the full dossier."

The name sat in the room with its edge out. Eleven years of client fields resolving to shells, and shells resolving to nothing — and at the bottom of the one wire that mattered, not nothing. A registrant. A building with a lobby, a reception desk, a payroll. On some floor of it, a person who had signed off, in writing, on nine months of him.

The morning had come full up in the alley. Through the window, at the north end, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see the edge of the mirror frame <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s crew had mounted to the wall, the angle adjusted twice this week by someone with strong opinions about angles. On the ledge above it sat the pigeon, which was, in point of fact, suspicious.

"Your client doesn't know about two of them," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> said.

"No."

"Which means your client isn't the biggest thing in this particular room." She stood, finally, and this time the coat went on with the ease of someone who'd finished what she came to do and had two more jobs before lunch. "I'll invoice you at sixty per scan. You'll forward it to the arrangement. It pays exactly — I know that about it already."

"It does."

"Good." She buttoned the third button, which was her tell for a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa8f-796a-8b70-7076ec482c7f">clean exit</entity>. "The protocol holds on one condition. You tell me the next time it asks you to do something like the carousel. Before. Not after, not in a logbook entry."

"Standard terms," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

She picked up her bag. At the door she paused — not the dramatic kind, the kind where something had arrived late.

"Somebody else has been reading your mail, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>," she said. "For months."

She was gone before the door finished closing.

The terminal chirped once, at 08:47, while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was writing the sixty-Φ line item into his payroll ledger. He wanted the ledger balanced and the drawer closed before the nine o'clock walk-through — clean books, clean desk, nothing left out to answer questions he hadn't been asked yet.

STANDING CONTRACT — UPDATE.
CLIENT NOTES THAT THE SCAN IDENTIFIED TWO MONITORING PARTIES BEYOND CLIENT'S ORIGINAL FLAG.
CLIENT IS REVIEWING.
CLIENT FINDS THE ARRANGEMENT HAS ALREADY PAID FOR ITSELF.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTES THE FIXER STRUCK CLAUSE THIRTEEN IN FOUR SECONDS.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT IS FILING THIS UNDER: GOOD PAPER.

Below it, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> added the new line:

SABLE — COUNTER-SURVEILLANCE — Φ60/SCAN.

He closed the ledger and slid it back in the drawer, next to the lock-spec file with the practiced fold, and the logbook entry that said WE LIVE UNDER A TYRANNY.

The drawer was getting full.

The next morning's logbook came under the door at 07:02, the paper still cold from the stairwell. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it at the kitchen table over the last of his tea.

07:00 — SHIFT START. WEATHER: COLD, DRY. LOGGED AS: RARE.
07:01 — NORTH ALLEY CLEAR. SOUTH ALLEY: THE PIGEON IS BACK. RAFTERS SAYS SAME PIGEON. DENTS SAYS PIGEONS ARE UNKNOWABLE. LEFT UNRESOLVED.
07:08 — WOMAN. CHROMATOPHORE LEGS, TWO SPONSORSHIP PANELS CYCLING. STOPPED UNDER THE WINDOW. LOOKED UP. NOT AT THE CAMERA — AT THE WINDOW. SHE KNOWS THE WINDOW. FLAGGING: NOT A PIGEON.
07:09 — BOSS, YOU HAVE A CALLER. — B.

Two entries, one person. A stranger who could pick his window out of a wall of them, standing in the alley at 07:08 and knocking by 07:09. The tea went down half-finished, still warm against his palm, and he was on the stairs before he'd finished deciding to be. Downstairs by 07:14.

Downstairs, the alley door was propped with the brick that lived there for that purpose. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> stood inside it, not outside — she'd let herself as far as the mat and stopped, which told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> something about how she'd been raised, or trained, or both.

Her chromatophore panels were running a <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7aa-7ce2-8a57-5b78e5c63d88">Ferrogate Transit</entity> ad at half-brightness — the legal minimum, which meant she had opinions about the sponsor and no way to fire them except that.

"<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

She looked at him a moment. Then: "You know my name."

"I looked you up after the box truck." He had. A courier registered under <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> Mensah, five-year license, clean filings — the kind of rider who sponsors a pair of display legs on a twelve-month rotation deal instead of leasing something off the rack. Which meant she was in the trade for real, and priced her gear that way. "You're calling the favor."

"I need to call the favor." Her voice had the flatness of something carried too long in one position. "Today. My brother loads cargo at Blackwater Receiving, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> freight yard off the 103rd interchange. A debt-court filing came in four days ago. They're saying he skimmed a container — forty-two units of med-grade microprinters. Twelve thousand wholesale. Docking six thousand from his pay. First hearing in three days."

"You looked into the filing yourself."

"I looked into everything," she said. "That's what I do. I don't call in a favor on a feeling."
